# Research question

How do complaint type, borough, timing, and location relate to the time the New
York Police Department (NYPD) takes to close NYC 311 noise complaints? The
analysis focuses on complaints created from June 30 through July 6, 2024 and
uses a two-hour closure threshold as the binary modeling outcome.

The source is NYC Open Data's
[311 Service Requests from 2020 to Present](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/erm2-nwe9).
The repository includes a fixed CSV snapshot so the results below do not change
when the live dataset is revised.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
from pathlib import Path
import sys

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

PROJECT_ROOT = Path.cwd()
sys.path.insert(0, str(PROJECT_ROOT / "src"))

from analysis import (
    DATA_PATH,
    clean_complaints,
    fit_response_model,
    load_raw_data,
    response_summary,
    test_group_differences,
)

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 12)
pd.set_option("display.width", 100)
```

# Data cleaning

```{python}
#| label: load-clean
raw = load_raw_data(DATA_PATH)
complaints, audit = clean_complaints(raw)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Measure": [
            "Raw rows",
            "Duplicate unique keys removed",
            "Rows with invalid/missing dates removed",
            "Rows with negative response times removed",
            "Analysis rows",
        ],
        "Count": [
            audit.raw_rows,
            audit.duplicate_rows,
            audit.invalid_date_rows,
            audit.negative_response_rows,
            audit.analysis_rows,
        ],
    }
)
```

Column names are normalized to snake case, dates are parsed explicitly, and
records without a valid creation/closure pair are excluded. `unique_key` is
used for de-duplication. ZIP codes remain strings so leading zeroes cannot be
lost. Unlike the earlier draft, this workflow makes no live geocoding calls and
does not rely on the obsolete `uszipcode` database.

```{python}
#| label: data-quality
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Field": ["borough", "complaint_type", "incident_zip", "latitude", "longitude"],
        "Missing": [complaints[c].isna().sum() for c in [
            "borough", "complaint_type", "incident_zip", "latitude", "longitude"
        ]],
    }
)
```

# Descriptive analysis

```{python}
#| label: overall-summary
overall = complaints["response_time_hours"].describe(
    percentiles=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95]
)
overall.to_frame("Response time (hours)").round(2)
```

Response times are right-skewed, so medians and interquartile ranges are more
representative than means. The figure caps the display at the 99th percentile;
all valid rows remain in the statistics and model.

The median closure time is `{python} f"{complaints['response_time_hours'].median():.2f}"`
hours, and `{python} f"{complaints['over_two_hours'].mean():.1%}"` of complaints
take at least two hours to close.

```{python}
#| label: response-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of NYPD noise-complaint closure times. The x-axis is limited to the 99th percentile for readability."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
cap = complaints["response_time_hours"].quantile(0.99)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(
    complaints.loc[complaints["response_time_hours"] <= cap, "response_time_hours"],
    bins=35,
    color="#28666e",
    edgecolor="white",
)
ax.axvline(2, color="#b23a48", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="Two-hour threshold")
ax.set(xlabel="Closure time (hours)", ylabel="Complaints")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: borough-summary
borough_summary = response_summary(complaints, "borough")
borough_summary.round({"median_hours": 2, "mean_hours": 2, "over_two_hour_rate": 3})
```

```{python}
#| label: complaint-summary
complaint_summary = response_summary(complaints, "complaint_type")
complaint_summary.round({"median_hours": 2, "mean_hours": 2, "over_two_hour_rate": 3})
```

```{python}
#| label: borough-plot
#| fig-cap: "Share of complaints closed in two hours or more, by borough (95% normal-approximation intervals)."
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.3
plot_data = borough_summary.sort_values("over_two_hour_rate")
rate = plot_data["over_two_hour_rate"]
se = (rate * (1 - rate) / plot_data["n"]).pow(0.5)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.barh(plot_data["borough"], rate, color="#7c9885")
ax.errorbar(rate, plot_data["borough"], xerr=1.96 * se, fmt="none", color="#1f2933")
ax.set(xlabel="Proportion closed in 2+ hours", ylabel="")
ax.set_xlim(left=0)
plt.show()
```

The Bronx has the largest observed two-hour rate
(`{python} f"{borough_summary.set_index('borough').loc['BRONX', 'over_two_hour_rate']:.1%}"`),
while Staten Island has the smallest
(`{python} f"{borough_summary.set_index('borough').loc['STATEN ISLAND', 'over_two_hour_rate']:.1%}"`).
These differences are descriptive and are not adjusted estimates.

# Group comparisons

Because closure times are strongly skewed, the analysis uses Kruskal-Wallis
tests instead of one-way ANOVA. The chi-square tests assess whether the binary
two-hour outcome is independent of each grouping variable. Cramer's V reports
effect size, which is more informative than a p-value alone in a large sample.

```{python}
#| label: inference
tests = test_group_differences(complaints)
test_display = tests.copy()
test_display["statistic"] = test_display["statistic"].map(lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")
test_display["p_value"] = test_display["p_value"].map(
    lambda value: "<0.0001" if value < 0.0001 else f"{value:.4f}"
)
test_display["effect_size"] = test_display["effect_size"].map(
    lambda value: "-" if pd.isna(value) else f"{value:.3f}"
)
test_display
```

These are associational tests, not causal estimates. A small p-value indicates
that the observed distributions differ, but it does not establish that borough
or complaint type causes a slower closure.

# Predictive model

A logistic regression predicts whether closure takes at least two hours. The
features are available when a complaint is created: borough, complaint type,
submission channel, hour, weekday/weekend status, and coordinates. The split is
stratified and reproducible. Numeric features are median-imputed and scaled;
categorical features are most-frequent-imputed and one-hot encoded. Class
weights reduce the tendency to predict only the majority class.

```{python}
#| label: fit-model
model_result = fit_response_model(complaints, random_state=42)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Metric": ["Accuracy", "Balanced accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1", "ROC AUC"],
        "Value": [
            model_result.metrics["accuracy"],
            model_result.metrics["balanced_accuracy"],
            model_result.metrics["precision"],
            model_result.metrics["recall"],
            model_result.metrics["f1"],
            model_result.metrics["roc_auc"],
        ],
    }
).round(3)
```

On the test set, the model's ROC AUC is
`{python} f"{model_result.metrics['roc_auc']:.3f}"` and its balanced accuracy is
`{python} f"{model_result.metrics['balanced_accuracy']:.3f}"`. Weighting the
classes raises recall for two-hour cases to
`{python} f"{model_result.metrics['recall']:.1%}"`, with lower precision as the
tradeoff.

```{python}
#| label: confusion-matrix
pd.DataFrame(
    model_result.confusion_matrix,
    index=["Actual <2 hours", "Actual 2+ hours"],
    columns=["Predicted <2 hours", "Predicted 2+ hours"],
)
```

```{python}
#| label: roc-plot
#| fig-cap: "Receiver operating characteristic curve on the held-out test set."
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(model_result.fpr, model_result.tpr, color="#28666e", linewidth=2,
        label=f"Logistic regression (AUC = {model_result.metrics['roc_auc']:.2f})")
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="#6b7280", linestyle="--", label="Random classifier")
ax.set(xlabel="False-positive rate", ylabel="True-positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1))
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: coefficients
pd.concat(
    [
        model_result.coefficients.nsmallest(6, "coefficient"),
        model_result.coefficients.nlargest(6, "coefficient"),
    ]
).drop_duplicates().sort_values("coefficient").round(3)
```

Coefficients describe conditional associations on the log-odds scale. They
should not be interpreted as causal effects, and the model should not be used
to rank neighborhoods or allocate enforcement resources without a fairness and
drift review.

# Conclusions and limitations

The typical complaint closes in well under two hours, but the distribution has
a long right tail. Two-hour closure rates vary substantially by borough, with
the Bronx and Queens above the citywide sample rate and Staten Island,
Manhattan, and Brooklyn below it. The group tests reject equal distributions,
although their effect sizes are modest. The logistic model has useful but
limited discrimination and should be treated as a descriptive baseline rather
than a production system.

Important limitations are:

1. Closure time is an administrative measure; it is not the same as time to
   resolve the underlying noise problem.
2. The seven-day sample may reflect a holiday-week pattern and cannot establish
   long-run seasonality.
3. Complaint records measure reports to 311, not the true prevalence of noise.
4. NYC Open Data can be revised after publication; the committed snapshot is
   therefore the reproducibility reference for this report.
5. Unmeasured operational factors may explain observed geographic differences.

# Reproducibility

The repository contains the fixed raw snapshot, data-download script, reusable
analysis functions, dependency specification, tests, and rendering commands.
Run `make test` to verify the transformations and `make render` to recreate this
